title: Paragraph Organization and Main Ideas

sections.eli10:
### Question 1

Picture a paragraph as an umbrella. The main idea is the fabric on top that covers everything underneath, and each supporting sentence is a rib holding up one section. A rib can be the most detailed part or the part you remember best and still only hold up a corner. So the test is not 'which sentence stands out?' but 'which sentence covers all the others?'

### Question 2

A topic sentence is the label on a storage bin. Before you dig through the bin, the label says 'winter hats,' so you know what should be inside, and the moment a soccer ball turns up you can tell it does not belong. The label does two jobs at once: it tells readers what is coming, and it tells the writer what to leave out.

### Question 3

Unity is a playlist where every song is the same genre: nothing feels out of place. Coherence is the order those songs are in, so the mood flows instead of lurching. That is why the two words are not interchangeable, because a paragraph can be perfectly unified and still land in a jumbled order that is hard to follow.

### Question 4

Imagine a roommate mentions the fridge is empty, the sink is stacked with dishes, and nobody has done laundry. No one says 'this apartment is a mess,' but you assemble that conclusion from the clues, which is an implied main idea. Had someone simply said 'this place is a mess,' the identical idea would be stated. Same idea, different delivery, and the delivery is the only thing that changes.

### Question 5

This is how a detective story works. You get the muddy footprints, the open window, and the missing necklace, and only on the last page do you hear 'the gardener did it.' Because the clues arrive first and the conclusion arrives last, you know not to grab the opening sentence and call it the main idea.

### Question 6

Think of stepping stones across a creek. The stones may all be solid, but if they sit too far apart you cannot cross, and words like 'however,' 'as a result,' and 'next' are the extra stones. One more habit that helps: in clinical writing, keep calling the same thing by the same name, so readers never wonder whether a new word means a new thing. Reaching for a fancier synonym may sound less repetitive, but it does not add any stones.

### Question 7

A topic is the name of the game; the main idea is the score. 'Shift-change handoffs' tells you which field everyone is playing on, but nobody can argue with a field. Add a claim about it and you suddenly have something worth five sentences of proof. A quick self-check: if you cannot answer 'I agree' or 'I disagree,' you are still holding the topic, not the main idea.

### Question 8

Try a quick game: cover one sentence at a time and ask, 'do the others explain this one?' The alcohol-rub sentence does not explain the audit sentence, and the audit sentence does not explain the soap sentence, so both fail. Only the hand hygiene sentence has all three of the others working for it, which makes it the sentence in charge.

### Question 9

A transition word is a bridge, not a magic wand. If two ideas sit on completely different islands, building a bridge just makes readers walk a long way to a place they never wanted to visit. The fix is to carry the stray idea back to the island where it belongs, which usually means a different paragraph or the delete key.

### Question 10

Picture a ladder. General ideas sit on the top rung and specific facts sit on the bottom rung. 'Communication matters' is way up top, so vague that you could spend a whole chapter proving it. 'Adherence rose at one clinic after teach-back' is down near the ground, where you can actually point at it. Details live low; main ideas live high.

### Question 11

Naming an implied main idea is like titling a photo album. If the pictures show a cake, balloons, and wrapped gifts, 'Birthday Party' fits every photo and invents nothing. 'Cake' covers only one picture, and 'Best Party in History' claims more than the pictures prove. Aim for the title that fits every picture and nothing beyond them.

### Question 12

Think of directions to a friend's house. Each step, such as 'turn left at the light,' can be perfectly clear on its own, yet if the steps arrive out of order you still end up lost. Topic sentences are the street names and the sequence is the route, and a section needs both. Trimming the directions shorter or making them more entertaining does nothing to get you there.
